stories.headline: Flood mitigation work in Chennai and suburbs to be completed by October 15
stories.title: Flood mitigation work in Chennai and suburbs to be completed by October 15
stories.summary: Work on storm water drain in Kosasthalaiyar basin is almost complete; 0.69 km will be completed in two weeks
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The State government has extended the deadline for completion of flood mitigation work in Chennai and suburban districts and has ordered civic agencies to complete the work by October 15.

At a meeting on Monday, B.Chandra Mohan, the Additional Chief Secretary/Commissioner of Revenue Administration reviewed the flood mitigation works and monsoon preparatory works for Chennai, Chengalpattu,Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram Districts in the presence of Commissioners of Chennai, Avadi and Tambaram Municipal Corporations, District Revenue.
Officials, WRD and Highway Officials.
The Commissioner of Revenue Administration also extensively reviewed various flood mitigation works and instructed to complete before October 15.
“The construction of a storm water drain network under ADB Scheme for Kosasthalaiyar basin is almost completed.
The balance 0.69 km will be completed in two weeks.
The priority works in Kovalam basin covering Sholinganallur, Perungudi, Alandur will be completed before the onset of Northeast Monsoon,” said an official.
In Chennai Corporation zones, desilting works are being carried out in 1,683 km of storm water drains.
Desilting has been completed in 1,328 km of drains so far.
The work is under way, and will be completed in one week.
Desilting works in 1.10 lakh silt catch pits were fully completed in the first phase.
In the second phase, desilting has been completed in 77,600 silt catch pits so far.

stories.headline: Tirupattur TVK MLA’s win by a single vote: Madras High Court rejects election petition filed against his victory
stories.title: Tirupattur TVK MLA’s win by a single vote: Madras High Court rejects election petition filed against his victory
stories.summary: Justice G.K. Ilanthiraiyan allowed an application filed by the MLA R. Seenivasa Sethupathy to reject the election petition preferred by former DMK Minister K.R. Periakaruppan
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Madras High Court on Monday (September 28, 2026) rejected an election petition filed against the victory of Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) MLA R. Seenivasa Sethupathy from Tirupattur constituency in Sivaganga district by a razor-thin margin of just one vote in the 2026 Tamil Nadu Asepolls.

Justice G.K. Ilanthiraiyan allowed an application filed by the TVK MLA to reject the election petition filed by Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) candidate and former Minister K.R. Periakaruppan, who contended that he lost the polls primarily because of the existence of two Legislative Assembly constituencies with the same name ‘Tirupattur’ in Tamil Nadu.
Mr. Sethupathy was declared elected on securing 83,375 votes as against 83,374 votes garnered by Mr. Periakaruppan.

However, the DMK candidate claimed a postal vote belonging to the Tirupattur constituency in Sivaganga district had been inadvertently sent to the Tirupattur constituency in Tirupattur district and that the wrongly transferred vote was not sent back to the right constituency.

Listing out the reasons for seeking a rejection of the election petition, senior counsel V. Raghavachari, assisted by advocates Dixita Gohil and Pranjal Agarwal, argued the election petitioner had presented a “highly implausible” scenario of a postal vote belonging to one constituency having been sent to another constituency just because of their identical names.

He contended the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961, make the identity of the intended constituency extremely difficult to lose by pressing into service multiple independent identifiers, which could enable the authorities to determine the constituency to which a postal ballot belongs.

The counsel pointed out the Tirupattur constituency in Tirupattur district was identified as constituency number 50, whereas the Tirupattur constituency in Sivaganga district was identified as constituency number 185.
He asserted that the constituency number, and not the name, was the key identifier.

He said every voter who intends to exercise his/her franchise through the postal ballot must make an application, using Form 12, to the Returning Officer concerned and therefore, the constituency gets determined emphatically even before the issuance of a postal ballot to an elector.

Further, the postal ballots have the full address of the Returning Officer of the relevant constituency pre-printed, without the need for the voters to fill it up by hand, and the postal covers too clearly mention the constituency name, number, district, and the full address of the Returning Officer.

“This means the postal ballot is not an anonymous page, which can ordinarily be treated as belonging to a constituency which happens to receive it by accident, coincidence, or otherwise,” Mr. Raghavachari said and added that it was the election officials who transport the postal covers.
The senior counsel also argued the election petitioner had not produced any material but for an affidavit filed by Tirupattur district DMK candidate.

stories.headline: Serious geopolitical developments create upheaval, desperation & concern in entire Pakistan
stories.title: Serious geopolitical developments create upheaval, desperation & concern in entire Pakistan
stories.summary: FRAGRANCE OF IDEAS Geopolitical developments taking place at a fast pace around the world, and particularly in the region and sphere in which Pakistan is involved, create great concern and desperation in Pakistan. These upheavals for Pakistan are mostly beyond any sort of control or convenient management that could have been ordinarily or even extraordinarily possible in routine matters. Analysts, government and their agencies throughout and the media in Pakistan are in serious and worrisome wild debate and discussion on these upheavals and the sudden developments causing perceivable hurt to its international and regional position. The SCO Summit in Uzbekistan followed by the BRICS Summit in New Delhi over the last two months have been a cause of serious concern and frustration for Pakistan. The tour of two Central Asian nations by PM Narendra Modi, followed by various programmes, diplomatic and political engagements therein, including his recognition by the Uzbek nation, conferring upon him their highest public honour, has also added to the already existing frustration. The uranium supply programme discussion with the Uzbekistan government by the Indian leadership has also been a migraine-giving factor for the think tank in Pakistan’s establishment. The success of the BRICS summit in New Delhi, in which Russian President Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping also participated with great enthusiasm along with the other global leaders, created ripples in the whole socio-political set-up of Pakistan. Moreover, Pakistan's non-inclusion in the summit due to the lack of any invitation further added salt to its injury. The invitation to Iran and serious engagements with them at the Summit was also not taken kindly by it. Ever since the outbreak of the US-Iran-Israel war, the energy crisis and their prices have disturbed the whole world. Every nation has made attempts to cater to its energy demand and is deeply concerned about the supply chain of oil globally. India has been continuously and consistently playing its positive role so far as the oil supply chain and its routes are concerned. It has maintained cordial and warm relationships with the Middle East countries for the good of humanity that includes its own good too. This was visible through the BRICS summit in New Delhi when the President of Iran had cordial bilateral meetings on its sidelines with the Indian side, in which he showed a great bonhomie and also exhibited positive expectations from the Indian leadership in the context of the US-Iran war. The positive overtures of the Indian side in this regard were taken due note of by everyone. India was also successful in brokering a high-level meeting between the UAE and Iran leadership during the BRICS sidelines, which sent shockwaves through Pakistan’s political leadership and its strategic policy managers. The Indian leadership has taken several important steps to ensure the stability of the oil supply chain through the Middle East despite the ongoing strife there. Besides ensuring crude oil and other energy supplies from Russia (despite US sanctions), Iran and Saudi Arabia, India took tangible steps to ensure its future energy requirements as well. In this connection, it went ahead with some important steps that have far-reaching implications regionally and globally. India and the UAE are taking their long-standing energy partnership to another level. Following India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to the UAE in May this year, Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Limited and Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) agreed to explore significantly expanding cooperation in strategic energy storage, including the potential storage of up to 30 million barrels of ADNOC crude oil in India’s Strategic Petroleum Reserves. This is surely significant as it ensures energy freedom to India in the region. The agreement is about expanding strategic storage cooperation and strengthening energy supply security between the two nations. Pakistan analysts and the media have been crying about this proposed cooperation, which also includes ADNOC’s participation in storage facilities at Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh (India) and the development of reserve facilities at Chandikhol in Odisha (India), alongside its existing storage presence at Mangalore. They feel surprised that the two sides are also exploring the possibility of storing crude oil at Fujairah in the UAE as part of India’s strategic petroleum reserve framework. Cooperation in LNG and LPG storage is also being explored by the two sides and the analysts in their opinion in Pakistan view it as a major threat to Pakistan in the event of any kind of conflict between India and Pakistan. They term it as 'a big disparity in the energy security scenario in the region that has negative implications for the region, especially Pakistan'. 'For a major oil-importing economy like India, that also exports refined oil to other countries globally, strategic petroleum reserves can provide an important buffer during wars, geopolitical tensions, shipping disruptions or other emergencies that affect global energy supplies'. Indian opinion in this regard says that larger and more diversified reserves can strengthen the country’s ability to respond to unexpected supply shocks. 'This is where diplomacy and security of energy come together, thus strengthening international partnerships today while preparing for the uncertainties of tomorrow'. While the India-UAE partnership shows how long-term energy cooperation can contribute to more resilient supply chains and greater surety about the future, Pakistan views the partnership as a threat to regional and global security. The Yemen Houthi rebels drone and missile attack targeting Saudi Arabia and its energy infrastructure, and particularly the city of Mecca, has created serious doubts about the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August this year between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. It has caused serious doubts about the collective security pact. Saudi Arabia was forced to take help from Israel in regard to the intelligence inputs regarding these and future attacks. The Agreement was put to the test, and it was observed that neither Pakistan nor Turkey could in any way come to the rescue of Saudi Arabia, particularly when the city of Mecca was under attack by the Houthis. The Agreement had said that 'any attack on any one of the signatories to the agreement would be treated as an attack on all of them'. The rebels also declared a naval blockade on the Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and Bab el Mandeb Strait, and there was virtually no response from Pakistan and Turkey in this connection, keeping in view the provisions of the Agreement between the three nations. The United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York in the context of its 81st session during the month of September 2026 brought India into focus once again. The Turkish President Erdogan and Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, besides Pakistan's permanent representative, raised the Kashmir issue in their addresses, which were responded well by the Indian representatives. However, the absence of the Indian Prime Minister, Chinese President and the Russian President from the UNGC session was also commented upon in various ways by the Pakistan analysts, while it was also said that the presence and address of the US President Trump in the UNGC had no major relevance in context of the current geo-political scenario. The support expressed in favour of India by the Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah and Bhutan Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay in the UNGC meetings and particularly the support for India's permanent position in the Security Council, was viewed very seriously by the analysts in Pakistan. The reply presented by a number of India's representatives on Kashmir had a great impact on the psyche of Pakistan's thinking minds. This can be further analysed in the context of the following development in which the Indian diplomat Khitij Tyagi serving as Counsellor at India’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations in Geneva, on September 23, 2026, delivered India’s Right of Reply during the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council, responding to Pakistan’s remarks on Jammu & Kashmir. One of the key issues he dwelt upon was the 1990 forced mass exodus of Kashmiri Pandits from the Kashmir Valley. Responding to Pakistan’s allegations concerning Kashmir, Khitij Tyagi said that Kashmiri Pandits were driven from their homes by the terrorists whom Pakistan had “armed, trained and sent across the border.” He added that the same terrorists subsequently killed Kashmiris belonging to different faiths. He also referred to reports of civilian deaths, arrests and shortages of food and medicine in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, and made it a point to convey that Pakistan ought to focus on development rather than territorial claims and the export of terrorism to the world and particularly to India. Ambassador Parvathineni Harish of India strongly rejected the Pakistan claims and said that Pakistan is habitually misusing the UN platforms for divisive political agendas and reiterated that the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are inalienable and internal part of India. Additionally, PM Sharief, in his address, raked up the issue of the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) at the UN again. However, the External Affairs Ministry of India, under the leadership of Dr S.Jay Shankar, External Affairs Minister, who was also at the UN, already issued a befitting reply from Bishkek in this context. India made its stand known to the world on the IWT issue. The statement said that the Hague-based International Tribunal ruling that 'India’s decision to suspend the Indus Waters Treaty was not legally permissible and that the 1960 pact remains fully in force' was not in any way acceptable to India. India rejected the ruling, saying the tribunal had no jurisdiction to pronounce on its sovereign decisions. India rejected the award and also the interim measures order, reiterating that it does not recognise the Court of Arbitration and has never participated in its proceedings. (The author is a senior BJP & KP leader, Human Rights Defender and a columnist and can be reached at: ashwanikc2012@gmail.com )

stories.headline: Supreme Court: Will fix timeline for FSSAI to enforce front-of-pack labelling
stories.title: Supreme Court: Will fix timeline for FSSAI to enforce front-of-pack labelling
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday refused to accept the timeline proposed by FSSAI for the implementation of front-of-pack labelling (FoPL) for food products, including four months' time for framing regulations and a 365-day voluntary implementation period for food businesses after notification, saying it was unreasonable and decided to fix the timeline for the food regulator.

A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran, however, made it clear to the regulator that it has to implement the court's order, which is in the national interest, in true spirit and not delay implementation.

It asked why the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) had fixed such a long timeframe to implement it as consultations with stakeholders had taken place in 2022." Why voluntary compliance for a year?...
Why do you want to start afresh with the exercise of hearing and calling for objections?

You started in 2022, what did you do in the last four years?" SC also termed advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi's plea for immediate implementation of FoPL as unreasonable and said it would pass an order to fix all contentious issues.
Additional solicitor general Brijender Chahar, appearing for FSSAI, said the process initiated in 2022 was relating to a star-rating system based on an entirely different criterion.
The bench, however, said the issue involved was very important and there should not be any more delay.
"We appreciate your initiative but there is a lot which is required to be done to give meaningful effect to what we want to achieve," SC said.
Reserving the order, SC told FSSAI, "Whatever order we now pass will be binding on you, and we expect you to implement it scrupulously.
We are undertaking this entire exercise for the good of the nation and for the good of citizens.
We will now pronounce the final order.
And we will keep it after some time to report due compliance in each and every direction.

stories.headline: Collegium picks Delhi high court chief justice, 2 others as SC judges
stories.title: Collegium picks Delhi high court chief justice, 2 others as SC judges
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'chief justice' in title weight 42
article_sentences: NEW DELHI: SC collegium Monday recommended to Union govt to appoint chief justices of Gujarat, Delhi and Telangana - Justices Sunita Agarwal, Devendra Kumar Upadhyay and Aparesh Kumar Singh - as judges of SC.
The collegium comprising CJI Surya Kant, and Justices Vikram Nath, B V Nagarathna, M Sundresh and P S Narasimha decided to recommend these three names.
On acceptance of the recommendation and issuance of warrants of appointments, SC's working strength will increase to 37 judges against the sanctioned strength of 38.
With Justice Agarwal's elevation, strength of women judges in SC would increase to two.
As the parent high court of Justices Agarwal and Upadhyay is Allahabad HC, its representation in SC would increase to four.
Justice Vikram Nath, who will be the next CJI in Feb, and Justice Manoj Mishra also started their judicial careers from Allahabad HC.
Justice Agarwal and Justice Upadhyay were appointed judges of Allahabad HC in Nov 2011 while Justice Singh was appointed judge of Jharkhand HC in Jan 2012.
Justice Agarwal became CJ of Gujarat HC in July 2023.
Justice Upadhyay was appointed CJ of Bombay HC on July 29, 2023 and then CJ of Delhi HC on Jan 21, 2025.
He held the first inquiry on discovery of burnt cash at Justice Yashwant Varma's residence in March last year.
Justice Singh was appointed Chief Justice of Tripura high court in April 2023 and then appointed CJ of Telangana in July 2025.

stories.headline: 68 high-risk glacial lakes identified in J&K
stories.title: 68 high-risk glacial lakes identified in J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sept 28: The Jammu and Kashmir Government has acknowledged the increasing risk of Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) in the Union Territory, attributing the growing threat to rising temperatures, accelerated glacier melt and expansion of glacial lakes. The government made the disclosure in response to an Unstarred Question tabled by Tanvir Sadiq, MLA Zadibal, in the Legislative Assembly. It stated that districts including Kishtwar, Ganderbal, Kulgam and Anantnag have been identified as areas facing GLOF-related risks. According to the government, the University of Kashmir has identified 616 glacial lakes across 12 districts, covering an area of 28.62 square kilometres, and has delineated 68 Potentially Dangerous Glacial Lakes (PDGLs) based on criteria laid down by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA). The government said a dedicated Core Committee was constituted through Government Order No. 71-JK(DMRRR) dated September 24, 2024, to undertake studies and formulate measures concerning high-risk glacial lakes. The committee subsequently categorised 24 high-priority lakes into Categories A, B and C based on 17 risk parameters. The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) has also mapped 546 glacial lakes covering 20.25 hectares, while the Central Water Commission, SDC and IITs have mapped and ranked several high-risk or highly susceptible lakes, including Gangabal, Kousar Nag, Harnag, Mundiksar, Hangu Lake, Boud Sar and Sheshnag. For real-time monitoring and early warning, the government said the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) has been nominated as the lead technical agency for designing and implementing an indigenous GIS-based GLOF Early Warning System. A Memorandum of Agreement with C-DAC is currently under process and is proposed to include water-level monitoring buoy systems with satellite communication, automatic weather stations, camera-based Glacial Lake Vision Units, and a web portal with a Spatial Decision Support System for real-time monitoring and dissemination of alerts. The government also said a UT-level GLOF Monitoring Committee was constituted under the chairmanship of the Principal Secretary, Home Department, in April 2024 to oversee glacial lake surveillance, satellite monitoring, field expeditions, risk assessment and mitigation. The committee has held five meetings so far. During these meetings, decisions were taken on scientific expeditions to high-risk lakes, standardisation of risk categorisation, preparation of GLOF-vulnerability inventories, development of district-level action plans, community awareness and integration of GLOF-related information into disaster management systems. The government said district-level teams have also been directed to undertake downstream Hazard, Vulnerability and Risk Assessments (HVRA) and prepare actionable GLOF risk-reduction plans. Coordination has additionally been initiated with ITBP and Armed Forces outposts located near high-risk lakes for operating manual early-warning networks to alert downstream areas in case of an emergency. On preparedness and evacuation, the government said District Disaster Management Authorities (DDMAs), SDRF and NDRF are mandated to conduct regular mock drills in vulnerable areas involving Aapda Mitra volunteers, line departments and local communities. The DDMAs have been tasked with preparing district-specific GLOF Action Plans, including downstream risk assessments, mitigation measures and response strategies. Authorities have also been directed to identify vulnerable villages, hamlets and critical infrastructure, besides mapping safe evacuation locations. The government further said vernacular awareness material provided by the NDMA and awareness campaigns led by the Rural Development Department are being used to sensitise Panchayati Raj Institutions and downstream communities about evacuation procedures and GLOF preparedness.
